data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense relies entirely on 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) to justify preferring better-corroborated theories without induction. However, the target fails to address the fatal logical incoherence of Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude, as demonstrated by Tichý and Miller. They proved that under Popper's own definitions, no false theory can be said to be closer to the truth than another; all false theories have the same verisimilitude value relative to the truth. Consequently, the mechanism described ('capturing more truth-content') is mathematically impossible within Popper's formalism. Without a working definition of verisimilitude, the preference for better-corroborated theories cannot be grounded as a 'non-inductive rule of action' and collapses back into the very inductive assumption the target claims to avoid: that past survival predicts future reliability or proximity to truth.
